To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a novel approach to longitudinal analysis of anatomical data that (a) is unbiased, (b) produces consistent, reproducible results, (c) is based on strong priors, and (d) is robust to noise.

(i) we present a new algorithm to transform and personalize group template information to a single subject's longitudinal time series data, (ii) we use this approach to estimate cortical thickness change and white matter volume change in a longitudinal setting, (iii) we evaluate this approach with both test-retest data and with a driving biological problem and find that it produces reliable and unbiased estimates of cortical thickness change and that when combined with sparse CCA it produces plausible, significant, and annualized decline in thickness and

we have developed a new method for longitudinal analysis of brain atrophy rates that is (a) unbiased, (b) produces low variance estimates of atrophy rates and (c) is robust and reliable in the context of longitudinal data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a robust, unbiased, longitudinal approach that can be used to study the progression of brain atrophy in neurodegenerative disorders and in normal aging.
the development of new, unbiased methods of longitudinal analysis for cortical and white matter volume change in neurodegenerative disease.
the use of penalized regression to produce a new approach for longitudinal analysis of cortical thickness.

the pipeline presented here produces a reliable, unbiased, longitudinal cortical thickness analysis pipeline.

our approach provides a new, robust, unbiased approach to longitudinal cortical and white matter volume and thickness change that is based on strong use and extension of prior information.
we have developed a pipeline for longitudinal analysis of cortical thickness and white volume that is (a) unbiased, (b) reliable, and (c) produces results with low variance.

we have developed a new method for longitudinal analysis of brain imaging data that provides reliable, unbiased estimates of change and that these methods can be used in a wide variety of applications.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we can reliably and accurately measure longitudinal change using sparse, multivariate, longitudinal methods and that these methods can be used to identify significant, annualized change in cortical thickness and volume in frontotemporal dementias.

a combination of diffeomorphic mapping and sparse penalized regression methods can be used to reliably estimate longitudinal change in cortical thickness and provide a framework for future work in this area.
the use of prior based, diffeomorphic registration can be combined with penalized statistical analysis to provide unbiased longitudinal estimates of cortical thickness.
